newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Sterling slide relieves pressure on Irish pound.
newsitem.headline: Sterling slide relieves pressure on Irish pound.

text.p: A three-pfennig slide in sterling following Labour's landslide victory in the British election has relieved some of the pressure on the Irish pound, allowing it to clamber back above 0.9300 sterling in early trade on Friday, dealers said.
"It certainly has alleviated some of the pressure. If sterling stays around these levels or weakens further, it solves a lot of problems for the Irish pound," one dealer said.
Sterling shed over three pfennigs in early trade as dealers took profits and trimmed long positions in the wake of the Labour Party's sweeping victory in the British elections.
Analysts said there was also some concern in the market about the size of Labour's likely parliamentary majority.

"A more moderate majority of 60 or 70 seats would have been taken quite well by the markets but Labour is seen to have been given an untethered hand with what they can or cannot do," Pat O'Sullivan, economist at AIB Capital Markets told Reuters.
Sterling/mark was trading at 2.7660 marks by 0748 GMT after trading close to 2.8000 yesterday.
This allowed the Irish pound to firm to 0.9325 sterling from 0.9180 at Thursday's close and a low of 0.9150 in recent days.
Analysts said the Irish pound was also helped by a half-point rise in official Irish interest rates late yesterday.
The Central Bank surprised the market when it announced that it was raising the official short-term facility rate to 6.75 percent from 6.25 percent with effect from May 2.
Its move came after two days of heavy selling of the punt which saw it lose around four percent of its value against the mark and three percent against sterling.
Analysts believe the sharp and sudden drop in the value of the Irish pound, particularly on a trade-weighted basis, fuelled fears of inflation at the bank, triggering the rate increase.

"The rate rise had an effect. It made it more expensive for overseas investors to sell the Irish pound and took some of the pressure off the currency but the key feature this morning is the weakening of sterling. That has eased the pressure considerably," AIB's O'Sullivan said.
Against the mark, the Irish pound dipped to 2.5590 this morning before recovering to 2.5775 marks by 0801 GMT, up from 2.5616 last night.
On the money markets, one-month money ticked up to 6.94/7.31 from 6.75/7.00 yesterday but dealers said this was a reaction to the current uncertainty.

"Rates are unlikely to stay up at these kind of levels but I don't think they will fall back dramatically either. What you will see is a normalisation of the yield curve to some extent," O'Sullivan said, adding he expected rates to settle around 6.50/6.75 percent at the very short-end.
